They also set the pace, but it was like they did too. We were getting about 100-odd crowns an hour. I don't remember exactly, probably around 115, something like that. And then we explored the subject, like, well, the contract, or rather the employment relationship, meant that we were not entitled to practically any social benefits, because it turned out that later the other couple we were with, so to speak, the girl got pregnant, and she had to wander around privately, visiting gynecologists and doctors. Later, they got everything sorted out properly so that they could be covered by Danish social security, but at first there was fear and uncertainty that they would be left on their own in the middle of nowhere, so to speak, far away from their families, but they managed to sort things out reasonably well. Well, these people were also imposing, you could say bossy. They couldn't stand opposition, and there was also fierce competition for the favor of the bosses, the management. And this fierce rivalry manifested itself in who was faster, who, who, who, who did more. Well, and just to get as many days as possible, as many hours as possible, having, so to speak, hourly work, they worked on a piecework basis, that is, simply whoever did more.

And I was one of those people, because for the lowest rate, around 170 kroner, I simply cleaned a huge silo of rust and waste, and it was terrible work. And I suspect that it was the same in the fields in Denmark, that the work we did was undervalued by at least half in terms of its remuneration, and I suspect that on a larger scale this may cause some social resentment, but on the other hand, what comfortable Scandinavian resident would take on such things if someone else can do it?

I came home and, well, my husband could tell you how I was mentally draining him, because I’m the stronger personality, and I was saying every single day, like, screw this, I don’t want to be here, I’m not staying, I’m not working in these conditions, I have a degree, I’ve done stuff, until the first payslip came. We invest all our resources in Poland. I think that is a significant benefit for this region, or for Poland in general. [...] Everyone is investing in some kind of property, or something similar. And of course, when you are building a house, you have to make all sorts of purchases. We do not buy those things in Germany. We buy them in Poland. So the local market benefits from that.

From what they told me, for example, well that we are hard-working, we are hard-working. They say to me, why are you running around so much, sit down, I'll make you some tea or something. Now is the time for a break, so we sit down and you can stay there for I don't know how long... One room to clean and they have a break. Recently, literally before we met, I had an emergency. The kindergarten called, my child wasn't feeling well, they suspected appendicitis. I carried him from the kindergarten to the hospital because he couldn't even walk. And then they told me, "We don't have a pediatric surgeon, we don't have a pediatric surgery department." They couldn't even do a full examination because there wasn't a doctor who could, well, give a conclusion—a pediatric surgeon, that is. Well, only a general practitioner, for example. And then the doctor asked me, "Can you take the child to the hospital in Opole right now?" I said, "I can't, I don't have a car." I started calling work, asking my coworkers if they could take me. And the doctor then got through to an ambulance, and we went to Opole. I do, but since our city is small, not all doctors are available. I have to travel to neighboring big cities, like Opole or Wroclaw, if I need anything. There's also this moment which is very interesting in Poland. It's easier with doctors in Ukraine. There aren't such long queues. Here, if you need to see a doctor, you can make an appointment and wait a maximum of two weeks. Here, the queues are so long. I had a situation with my child. He needed to have his adenoids and tonsils removed. And he had a doctor's referral. I called five hospitals, and they all told me the waiting list was three years. Three years. But my child needs his adenoids and tonsils removed. And he can't wait three years. I was forced to go to a private clinic. Well, luckily, my work gave me a deduction. And I paid for the removal in Opole, the surgery.

I worked as a furniture designer and as a designer of various bathrooms in a large tile hypermarket. I also worked as an interior designer. Now, at the moment, here in Poland, I've been in contact with companies and also doing some work remotely, well, just sort of in dialogue. First of all, the first thing I did when I came here to Poland, without knowing the language yet, was start searching online for the right CV for Poland. I used a translator—maybe it wasn't quite right at the beginning, broken, incorrect—but I started by writing my CV. And that CV helped me, I mean. Then, when I started learning the language, I realized I needed to rework it. I reworked it, and when I started sending my CV to job postings, I also started adding motivational letters. And that's how I looked for work. I think if I found at least some remote, short-term jobs, I think it means what I simply described in my CV was enough.

It was easy. There were designated spots for Ukrainian children. When I was looking for a place, I went to the government department, the department that deals specifically with education. The staff there were very helpful. They immediately called around the kindergartens and gave me a referral to a specific one that had told them there were spots. I went, and my child was enrolled right away. It was early spring. And literally a month later, my child started kindergarten. The adjustment process was, of course... Every child is different, but my child had a very difficult time adjusting. We even went to a psychologist, and they gave us a referral from the kindergarten to a clinic that specializes in psychology. We took tests there, had sessions with a psychologist, and then we were assigned to a psychologist at the kindergarten. And a speech therapist so he could learn Polish better and adapt faster. And after these sessions, the adaptation process began very, very quickly.

I wasn't able to attend any courses because they were in the evenings, and I had no one to look after my child. I learned the language myself online, through online courses, and I studied at work because I work with Poles.

At first, we were placed under the guardianship of this employer. We lived in the same building. It was a large private house, several floors, and several families lived there. Firstly, it's a small town, there were a lot of Ukrainians, and all the apartments were occupied. It was very difficult to find a free apartment at all. The second issue is the occasional contract. If you have a child, many landlords don't want to sign a lease agreement through a notary without this occasional contract. That was also a problem.

We came 8 people: me, my mother, my sister with two children, my niece with a child, and my grandson.We lived only in Olesno, because we had many children, three, at the time we left and therefore it was very scary to leave at random, three children and my mother was already at such a respectable age.We got an apartment here. First, the girls left, they returned, my sister, children, niece and nephew. I, my mother and my grandson stayed. We pay for the apartment ourselves, but it is social housing, we have a direct agreement with the government. It is not very suitable, because it is very small, 27 square meters, that is, a single's apartment, well, it really is not suitable, but we have nothing else. I pay for the apartment, it is quite expensive to maintain the apartment, because it is completely powered by electricity. We have heating, meaning radiators, water, we have bathroom heating, a stove, a kettle, it's all on electricity, that is, somewhere on average, my apartment costs a month, somewhere from nine hundred zlotys to 1,100 depending on the time of year. For such a small apartment, of course, taking into account the fact that I have a reduced payment for this rent. It's just very favorable for us who are not working, well, I understand what the figure sounds like. Many people say that this is nothing, but considering that it is 27 square meters, we do not have a full-fledged sleeping place, 3 people live, for us, of course, it is expensive for us at the moment.

To be honest, I have a problem with Polish. I also went to the courses and here it is. Well, to be honest, if, let's say, I attended general courses conducted by Mr. Myroslav. I will pay for the courses, I have no financial opportunity, because I have a 75-year-old mother and a grandson, who is already 3 years and 10 months old, respectively.

Of course, of course yes, but my main problem is the language, the main problem. That is, I need it. I have no possibility I could do it individually, if I had the opportunity individually. Well, it's understandable that it's perfectly normal in the store, I can calmly explain myself there, I can explain myself perfectly calmly in the same way. Well, with a translator, where I don't have enough spare words. Well, of course, this is the most superficial, the most basic level.

Well, not because the work is bad or good. Yes, let’s say I went to work there in the park zone and they offered me, I worked for 3 days. quote: My mother had an operation, her eye hurt very badly, very badly. And we went to see a doctor here in Olesno, to an ophthalmologist, and she suggested, looked, said that you have a very high risk that she may go blind, because the very high intraocular pressure, the first and second, the nerve is thinned by 20%, oh, I mean 20% of the nerve remains. And accordingly, at any moment, any wrong movement is sharp and she will simply go blind. That's why she gave an urgent direction to Wroclaw, and we accordingly... And we went to Wroclaw, to a paid clinic here, and I understand that Poland is very practiced, there is private practice and patients are served first by hospitals. Therefore, since the situation was critical, already urgent, requiring permission, we were taken. The operation was performed, we waited for a short time, about a month. Well, now it's a difficult rehabilitation period after that, because you have to go to Wroclaw again, it's 2 and a half hours there and 2.5 hours back. Plus, you have to register there at 6:00 a.m., so we have to go to Wrocław and rent an apartment for a day. In the morning, I go to register at 06:00, because if you get there later, you may not get there that day. Well, there are nuances

She lived in a boarding school here, where children study and live. She had rooms, 3 rooms. The three of us lived in that room for a year: me, grandmother and son, and then we found an apartment there. The Poles helped us, and now we are renting an apartment.

Well, like it or don’t like it, I have to work somewhere. Because there is nowhere to go to work here. It is true, thank God, that the Poles found me a job, that I have been working for a year. Because before that I worked as an intern, I was cleaning at a school. Then they offered me to go and work there for six months. Well, for the money, but they paid half. For example, they were paid a fixed rate there, and I was paid 1448 Polish zlotys, because I was like an intern, and I worked just like them, 8 hours. And I did the same work, it was just so annoying that they work, I work like them. I worked even more than they did. Because I went to work at 11, they came at 12, when I came at 11, I had to pull the grass near the school, sweep it, rake the leaves, I did everything. And they just sat there, then I worked in the yard for another hour, and then I came, I still cleaned the classrooms, and they came to school at 12. And they didn't go to the yard, they didn't do anything. Yes, everyone did their share. It was also so sad that no one helped you, that there was no one in the yard

We have a friend in Poland, and some Poles from work helped him out at night. They found this, like, school for priests in Krakow, right in the center of Krakow, in the middle of the night. I think I told you about it. And they put us up there, we stayed there for two or three days, so they fed us, and, of course, free accommodation. They gave us everything we needed, they helped us. And they found us a family, 20 kilometers outside of Krakow, in Jerzmanowice, who were willing to take in refugees. And that's how we ended up with Sandra. There was this family there—a husband and wife with three grown children. So they were willing to help as much as they could and as long as needed. We stayed with them for about four or five months. And then they also helped us find and rent an apartment in Krakow through relatives, because we couldn't find one ourselves due to the prices, the kaucja, we didn't have that kind of money, of course, even for two people. And she helped us find an apartment through relatives, we helped them do some cosmetic renovations, and they rented it out to us, let's say, for Krakow, for a nominal fee.

Then I started thinking about going back to work. I'm a family doctor by profession. I worked in Ukraine. I think it's been three years since my internship, and yes, there was work. So, I started looking around here to find out how I could get a job as a doctor. I tried inquiring in Krakow, but they were also offering me jobs at the hospitals, but they... Well, they wanted me to have documents, a confirmed diploma, and then they would hire me there eagerly. Also, at the very beginning, everyone there was very afraid of these termed rights to do the job, these temporary ones. No one understood anything, didn't know how it all worked. Basically, I didn't get it in Krakow.

When we were living with a family there in Jerzmanowice, a free basic course started with a Polish language teacher for refugees. So, we went there for more than a couple of months, maybe three. It was just the basics. Then, in June or July, well, in the summer, I found an online medical course for refugee medics. So, I also left my documents, confirmation from when I arrived, my diploma, a photocopy, and there was also a free course for a couple of months, specifically with a medical focus. That's it, and then I learned everything on the job.

Let's start with the fact that I was initially struck by the number of refunded tests patients can get for free. They have a much broader range of blood tests than we do. For example, we have morphology, sugar, I don't know, cholesterol, and liver function tests aren't always in question. They also include thyroid function. For men, they can check PSA for prostate cancer. So, there's a wider range of these free tests, which can be done once a year. And if needed, if there are indications, the doctor can prescribe as many as needed. So, if a patient is sick, I can usually prescribe morphology or inflammation tests 3-4 times a year, as needed. And the patient won't have to pay for it. Speaking of medications, there are also a lot of them, despite some Poles complaining, but in general, patients, what do they need? All medications are completely free. In fact, there are also a lot of free medications, including those from reputable companies. If we compare it to Ukraine, well, honestly, at first, there were mostly these refunded medications—I can't remember what they were called in Russian—refunded, compensated. There were some companies there, well, not so much, like health, pharma, and other things, which had more chalk than active ingredients, and these medications didn't really work. Here, however, there are very good companies, all using refunds. And in reality, when it comes to medications, there's no such thing... There are no complaints about any medications, everything always works, antibiotics, I don't know, blood pressure, and so on. We, too, have sometimes encountered problems with certain medications not working, but that simply speaks to the quality of the drugs. What else? Well, the big problem here, of course, is with specialists. That means huge, very long lines to get a free consultation with a specialist. For a cardiologist, the wait is about a year. For an endocrinologist, we're currently booked for 28 years in Olesno. And patients have to go privately, because if it's a new diagnosis, then specialized testing and a specialist consultation are needed. Obviously, you have to pay for specialist consultations. Well, as I've been told, yes, it's quite expensive. About 300 zlotys, give or take, depending on the specialist. 300-400 zlotys plus, that is, you pay for each appointment. But it's expensive.

Well, I didn't come to Warsaw, I came straight to Olesno, because my daughter was offered a job here. And here we are together, here is a private house, well, to take care of a woman, a woman with Alzheimer's

quote: But since there is no definite return, because we only go there for a month or 6 weeks, we are attracted to this place because our home is here. We got used to our surroundings, neighbours, our life. I am not really uncomfortable, I love my country, Turkey. Both the Netherlands and Turkey. For example, if I lived in Turkey for 25 years, it has been 30 years in the Netherlands. It's more. But I also have memories of my childhood in Turkey. But in the end, I want to come back to the Netherlands.

We still embrace each other here, no matter where we are from. We are always together. The mosque is a different thing. We have day groups. We go on outings like... Was it last July? Last summer 50 of us travelled to The Hague with train tickets. All of us. Imagine that. We'd go on mass trips like that. We'll go to Germany once or twice, to the bazaar and so forth. It's nice. We're used to it. As they say, we're Germans [Alamancı] in Turkey. German [Alamancı] there, foreigner here. It really is, but you can't be from there either. Here, even if you say you're from here, there are still people who don't accept it. But I'm half and half. Half and half.

I said to the teacher, I've been coming here for years, I've been attending language courses, summer courses, I said I want to learn in a more capable way. I said I want to do everything myself. By the way, there was an Inburgering (Dutch Integration Course) before, but it exploded across the Netherlands. I went then, I went for a year, I already knew a lot. They said it would be difficult, they said it was difficult, difficult, difficult. They scared us so much. I was always the first to go to there for the exams. I said it wasn't difficult at all.

My cousin, for instance, I get on really well with him. We're about the same age group. And I went on holiday with him to Bodrum once we were in Turkey. And he also came to the Netherlands once and then we came here. Yes, I actually let him tour a bit. Showed the Netherlands.

If you grow up as a generation with few people of a different colour in your class or a different religion, you're not used to that. And the generations that follow have. And then you normalise, you can only normalise. And that is where these, this city for instance, is still very much lagging behind if you compare it to big cities for instance.
Our neighbour now sees us as people who have always lived there and belong. And now the new newcomers, are the new invaders and people who don't belong and the strangers so to speak.

What most Turkish people do, and I'm talking about my mother's generation. They come together once in a while, for example such a Gün (day). People come together at home and the host takes care of the food. They collect money and then kind of help each other actually. Every time you go somewhere, you give €100 to that person and when everyone comes to you, you get all that money back, for example. So in that way people still speak to each other often.

Two of my children started school. The school provided children carers. They looked after them in a room at school. We had lessons in another room. I went to those language classes for 3 or 4 years, probably once a week for 3 hours. Then the children learnt from school and by reading the subtitles on the television. We started going to the neighbours, drinking coffee and talking. The children were playing all together on the street. They would go there and eat. They would come to me and eat. And so on and so forth.

I suffered a lot from my in-laws. Not in terms of fights, but financially. I mean, the situation was like that. They were relatives. In terms of their financial situation, they had fields in the village [in Turkey]. But there was no father, no one working. Since my husband was the eldest, all the burden was on him. I had a lot of trouble. He used to support them financially. Half of half a loaf of bread will be divided. Because he has to. He has a mother and three unmarried siblings. Just her pension. They can barely feed themselves from the fields.

We had a certain line what we had to say when I was working in the tourism sector in Turkey. It seemed like we could offer work to the villagers there. That was true. [...] But [it] was played a bit like that, as if we were holding people back there so that they they would stay there to find work instead of moving to big cities and from there to Europe, so to make people stay [in Turkey]. And then that was the line: We offer people work here, so if you start buying here then the ball will start rolling. [...] It's a very nice place to work, though, because most of my colleagues came from Europe. And of course they were trying to find a place there and we understood each other. And the visitors who came were surprised by how well my Dutch is. And they gave me liquorice, you know, things like that because I missed that. And that was really nice work.

Sometimes my mother also worked. She worked for six years in a row and in addition, she worked occasionally because she sat with us. But I just notice that those times. They had a very hard time, only they were welcome because they were brought here. Now we are no longer welcome. Now they just want us gone. Us yes, foreigners or you see that right-wing party being elected, right? So I assume then that people, the majority, have trouble with foreign people. We don't actually belong anywhere. I mean about the second generation then. You might feel at home here, but we don't belong in the Netherlands, but we don't belong in Turkey either. In Turkey, they say Almancı, and here they say, you came from. Wherever I have worked, oh how well you can speak Dutch, how different your name is. Where are you originally from? That's always question number one. Always it is asked. I think they had easy jobs and a lot of things were easy to get into, to learn Dutch. My mother had a teacher at home. And now I have a daughter-in-law who is from abroad and she is studied. She's a stylist, she can speak good English and her own native language. She just got there and she has to pay €3,000 for 3 years of Dutch language courses. And then they go and see if you are advanced and then I think what the hell do you know? How crooked! You don't give her anything anymore because you don't have any ‘money’. Now she has to learn on her own. She has bought books. Because she doesn't get the money for it. And they are just starting out in their lives. My son is a high school teacher, but he couldn't do his job because it was just 12 hours and he wants to bring his wife here and then he has to have a one-year contract and have a certain salary. So then he can't do his job, he goes to work at a factory to bring his wife here. It's just a very strange world. In our parents' time, everything was given and you were welcome. You did the dirty work, thank you very much. And now we are actually a burden to them. “They don't leave anymore. They are no longer guest workers, they are settled here and only more are coming.”

quote: They had that tendency to keep going back. That was always a talk of the day. Well, saving money, oh, we shouldn't buy something new. Second-hand, because yes, when we go back, where should we take it? How can we take it with us? That's how you used to hear. That's how you lived too. You lived every time with the idea of. Oh, we'll go back sometime. We didn't get new bikes, second-hand, because there was no money for that, because my father worked alone. And my father did make sure we went to Turkey every year so we got to know our family and the language. We also only spoke Turkish at home.

quote: Let there be fair opportunities. See people's effort. See that they go to school and give them a chance. Don't just look at diploma but also background. Look at capacity. A person does not consist only of a diploma. Why can't you hire the person? It is not because the person is not intelligent but only because it was not allowed. That opportunity has been taken away from her hand. Try to look beyond that piece of paper. Look at what people did before, did now and after. Tackle it more comprehensively.

My father was a cattle herder, I was eight years old and my brother was six years old. When my father came here, my mother, me and my younger brother were herding cattle, he got dressed without saying goodbye to us and came here quickly. The jacket was from someone else, shoes from someone else, my uncle's jacket, shoes from one of the relatives, the conditions were not good.

quote: There were no Turkish things here. I opened the first Turkish food company in this city.

[owner of a food company:] The customers are mostly Dutch. 99% Dutch. I already have the Dutch mentality. I open on time and close on time. I never compromise my work. I have such a habit. I go half an hour earlier, but I don't stay more than half an hour. I have such a discipline towards myself.

[owner of a food company:] At first I suffered a lot from the municipality. They wouldn't give me permission where I could stop. They wouldn't give me permission, they said they didn't have any. I travelled from market to market for five or ten years. When I was working at work, I used to look at the newspapers during my break. I would immediately go to the chief. My boss helped me a lot. The Dutch helped me a lot. They also helped me a lot financially while I was setting up this business. When I needed financial support, I would go to the boss and he would say okay, but look, 40 people work here, you won't call out to anyone. I would ask for 750 or 1000 euros and he would have no problem with it. I would ask him to cut it from my salary, or if it was too much, I would say cut it from there, and he would do it. So he was very interested. In order for my business to grow, he would bring 40 people so that I could make money. The food was good, of course. They have helped me a lot. I'll never forget their kindness.

But now language is a must. It was different in my father's time. But now, for example, there are newcomers who come with the logic that Europe is very good. They think that they can buy a car in Europe for two or three months. But look, all the young people who come here have difficulties. As we have heard, there is no such thing as coming here and finding a job immediately. I asked someone do you think that they are waiting for you? What business will people have with you? You didn't complete your education in Turkey. You are twenty years old. You have no education. You don't speak any English, let alone Dutch. What business do I have with you? Nothing. In my father's time there were more physical jobs. Because my father was very brave. He also did physical labour. Nowadays people say they don't want to work in a factory. English at the desk. People are not waiting for you to come and sit down. They think too easily.
topic_additional: Education, Language barriers, Work/employment, Motivations to migrate

quote: I've wanted to buy a house in Germany it since I was a kid. We live 15 minutes from here. We are right on the border. Since I was a child, we had family in Germany and Austria and I saw that their houses were big. Cars were cheaper. It was more advantageous financially. Instead of paying 600 euros for the car I use here, I pay 400 euros in Germany. For example, we can do shopping for a maximum of 80 euros. Everything is included. In the Netherlands you pay at least 150 euros for it.

Dutch people are different. Here, I can walk very easily in the bazaar with my wife, but in a big city where there are many foreigners I feel more uncomfortable. Dutch people are cooler, they are not interested in what others do. But the behaviour of foreigners is worse.
In the last five years the municipality here has been voted the worst municipality and unemployment has increased a lot. There are very few job opportunities.

I always took the initiative myself in the [life]story I just told. Always learning a language, finding a job, joining life as soon as possible, doing something as soon as possible. Because this increases your self-confidence as soon as possible. Also, you know, when you are like this, you have a responsibility. You have a spouse, children, you are starting a family, a good future. The conditions in Turkey were very good. Now you are trying to rebuild everything from scratch. Making a new mistake. When that happens, everything is very difficult. I told myself that if I start as soon as possible, I will get through this process much faster. Yes, I believe that I have found a really good job through this work-study project. My environment consists of very good, very high quality people. In other words, I can say that I was able to find a job that is almost similar, maybe the same as the job I was doing in Turkey. This, so to speak, is not everyone's fortune due to these difficult conditions. I am not talking about a personal talent or character, because there are many obstacles you have to overcome.

I think it is enough to do a little research rather than a conscious choice. Because especially if you are going to Europe, if you do not have any support at first, if you do not have the means to stand on your own feet, you choose countries where the social state is at the forefront. It makes more sense to choose. Because why? You will definitely need support when you first start your life. This was the Netherlands because it is a state with a strong social aspect. Maybe it could have been Germany, maybe Belgium, I don't know, maybe Switzerland. In other words, the Netherlands is a particularly prominent country in Europe, or a strong country economically. Also, the progress of the official procedures of the immigration process varies in each country. For example, in the Netherlands you apply for citizenship after 5 years, in Switzerland you apply after 10 years, and so on. When you consider such things, there are pros and cons.
topic_additional: Income, Integration, Legal barriers, Motivations to migrate

quote: We sell mainly Turkish products. And yes, sometimes people are curious about that, non-Turkish people. And then I explain some things. Or then they are looking for something. If they don't know how to use it, or if they are looking for something sweet, I just suggest Turkish things. We have baklava, we have Turkish fruit. They like that.

The advantage of growing up here is that you have a better command of the language than people from other cities, I think. If you talk to primary school children here, who compared to other primary school children in big cities, you name it. I think the children here learn the language better. Better command of the language which also makes you not stand out.
Now I don't prefer living in big cities at all. The air and water here is better. We live in a house with a garden, not in an apartment. There is no such opportunity in big cities.

For example, we don't come here to shop. We go to Kayseri. Kayseri is close to here. I buy this for 50 TL in Kayseri. I come here, and it's 200 TL. Because there's a difference of about 150 TL. Okay, their money gains value when they come here, but they also say, “Why should we always spend all our money here?” Then they go elsewhere. But if this price stayed the same, this place would develop much more. Because, as I said, there are a lot of Germans in Akdağmadeni, and when they come, they leave all their euros, foreign currency, everything here. Because one person who comes can easily spend 10,000 euros and leave. Well, what happens is, this benefits us. If they didn't mess with people's things like that, as I said, Akdağmadeni would really rise above its district status. It would grow a lot. It would grow like Sivas. Like that. But as I said, the people in Akdağmadeni are hungry, so to speak, because they are a little behind, so we can sell it at a slightly higher price and make a better profit. But if they sold it at a lower price, they would have more opportunities, but they don't know that. So, I don't know, maybe that's why they contribute.

MIGRANT: Exactly, of course. When I came here, I didn't know much Turkish. Now I'm used to the language there. (laughs) INTERVIEWER: I'm curious about that. That's why they enrolled him in 8th grade. So what did you do about Turkish here? Did you go to a course or something? Did you take extra classes? Private lessons?MIGRANT: No, I definitely didn't take any because I was with my friends at school. For example, I didn't know what a pen was. I'd ask my friends, “What do you call this?” and they'd make fun of me.

So did I want to go? Well, yes, we wanted to go. I didn't have this huge desire to go. I mean, I never said, “I absolutely have to go.” But since our dad was there, and our folks went, we went too, taking that opportunity. I had already seen it in movies, you know, Hollywood movies, European movies. The houses are beautiful, the roads are beautiful. The landscaping is done. The surroundings were beautiful. When I landed there, it was like a postcard in my mind. Seeing it shaped my mind about that place forever. I never wanted to stay there anyway. I just wanted to find an opportunity to come back. We are building here….Iron in the construction sector. We always give checks at the place where we shop, or we borrow something. We pay the check a month later. We definitely pay the money. I remember a lot because, I don't know if you'd call it traumatic, but after we moved here, my childhood was spent constantly missing that place. Constantly missing it. Because there were so many things here that weren't there. You know, Karaman is a small town, and in 2007, it really wasn't a developed city at all…was like a village, and even though I was a child, we came to Karaman from a metropolis like Amsterdam. It was very difficult even for a nine-year-old child, I can say that. I was bored, I missed my friends there, I missed going out. Because we used to go out a lot with my dad there. I don't know, because it was a big city, our house was very close to Amsterdam's central station. Whenever we got bored, we would go out. We would take the tram, the metro. We would go on trips. To all kinds of different places in Amsterdam. Then I came here. There weren't even buses in Karaman. I mean, there weren't even municipal buses. There are these local minibuses, but that's about it. There was nowhere you could go like that. I mean, things that interest a child in the Netherlands, like entertainment, going out, parks, and then eating and drinking, where the range of food and drink in the markets is very, very wide, huge, different…

My brother-in-law used to bring a bicycle back then. He came by car a lot. He's my sister-in-law's husband. I said, let's get a bicycle from my brother-in-law [her husband's name]. I don't know, water bursts there, they dig there, it gets muddy. I sat down and cried. I sat down and cried out of anger... My mom was like that too. They were changing our things, our lines. We came a year later, they were changing the lines, they dug up everything. The bike, I don't know, I think it's like the soil there. You ride the bike on top of the soil there. It doesn't stick... We couldn't save any money. It was very difficult. I told my wife, one day I want to go back. Because a law had been passed in the Netherlands. They passed a law called the 45-year-old law. They said we would give a salary of 600 euros to those who returned to Turkey. Or there were a few other countries too. I wanted to take advantage of such an opportunity. I said, I gathered the kids. Look, we want to return to Turkey. If you want to come, come with us. If you don't want to come, we'll find a way to settle you here, and we'll go like that. I thought the economy here would be better, that it would be easier. That was our plan, our program... Because 2014 was ending, we had to finish before 2014. More precisely, we had to apply before 2014. And I called him. The kids said, “Dad, you're right.” May God be pleased. If we were in your place, we would have gone too. Because if life here is going to be better, why should I wait for that?
